note: Gate stack for a TypeScript project (tsc + eslint + vitest). Copy to gates.json at the repository root, then delete gates you do not have. The arch and mutation gates carry output assertions — read their `why` before you change them.

gates.name: types
gates.why: the code is well-formed and typed

gates.name: depth
gates.why: no NEW shallow method, pass-through method, comment that repeats its line, or declaration comment narrating the implementation. Four of Ousterhout's fourteen red flags: the four that are decidable from the source text. The other ten are judgements about meaning, and a metric that guesses at them gets ignored — those belong to jo-7, with a reviewer reading. Findings are ratcheted against .depth-baseline.json, so this gate means 'never worse than the baseline': create that file once with `depth --update-baseline` after reading what it accepted. A missing baseline is an error, not a pass, because a ratchet with nothing to ratchet against is a gate that checked nothing. Advisory until that first triage pass: these are heuristics on prose, and an unread wall of findings is how a real gate gets muted. Arm it by deleting this line once the baseline has been read.

gates.name: unit
gates.why: the named behaviors hold, and this emits the coverage file the crap gate reads

gates.name: crap
gates.why: no function is both complex and under-tested. Must run after unit.

gates.name: dry
gates.why: no duplicated block above the threshold

gates.name: arch
gates.why: dependencies point where the architecture rules say they point. The `expect` is load-bearing: dependency-cruiser cannot load the TypeScript compiler on TypeScript 7, so it cruises zero modules, prints 'no dependency violations found' and exits 0. Without the assertion that silent pass is a green gate that checked nothing.

gates.name: mutation
gates.why: the assertions detect changed behavior. Slow — run it deliberately, and scope it: `--mutate <paths>` (a tree, a file, or a line range like `src/core/plan/direction.ts:120-180`) is what bounds a run, and `--incremental` is what makes the next one cheap — pass both. `--incremental` alone is a cache, not a scope: Stryker documents it as "store results in a file and use that file to speed up the next run", so a cold cache with no `--mutate` is the whole sweep, hours of it. Let the gate's own timeout do the timing: a run cut short by a shorter deadline reports nothing and reads exactly like a pass. Two ways this gate lies, both documented in templates/stryker.conf.cjs: Stryker's vitest integration reports every mutant as survived (the `reject` pattern names it) — templates/stryker-vitest-runner.mjs is the fix for that, `templates/stryker.conf.cjs` ships it, and it is what makes `coverageAnalysis: "perTest"` usable — measured at 3m39s -> 22-40s on a real 1196-file project through `mutate-changed`, same verdicts, with checks/test_mutation.sh pinning the shipped template and both runners against a fixture whose one undetectable mutant must survive. `gates --init` writes the plugin next to the config; the project still needs `npm i -D @stryker-mutator/vitest-runner` — and a command runner left at its default concurrency times every mutant out and reports a 100% score made of nothing but timeouts. The `concurrency` and `timeoutMS` settings in the template are what stop the second.
